newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bangkok subway contract to be signed soon-agency.
newsitem.headline: Bangkok subway contract to be signed soon-agency.

text.p: A contract to build Bangkok's first subway system will be signed before Thailand's November 17 general election, the director of Thailand's Mass Rapid Transit Authority (MRTA) said on Wednesday.

The Office of the Attorney General would submit a contract to the MRTA and the Overseas Economic Co-operation Fund, the Japanese project financier, for approval this month, Theerapong Attaijarusit told Reuters.
If suitable, it could then be signed by the contractors, he said.

The contractors are concerned a new government in Thailand might order a review of the US$950 million project, one of the last to be approved by the outgoing administration of Banharn Silpa-archa in late September.
The subway is seen as a key component of plans to break Bangkok's urban traffic gridlock.

"The consortium would like to have this signed as soon as possible," said Oku Oka, manager of consortium member Tokyu Construction, "But the thought of a change of government is then a very, very big problem."
Teerapong said such concerns were justified but interference was unlikely.
"If you ask if they have the authority to change this then yes they do, they are the government, but I don't think so at this stage," he said.
"I don't think anyone will do anything different."

But work-sharing negotiations between the consortium members responsible for the 11 kms (seven miles) first stage of the subway, running from the city centre into the eastern suburbs, are described by project officials as difficult.

After two weeks of negotiations the parties, Thai construction firm Ch Karnchang, Germany's Bilfinger and Berger and Japan's Kumagai Gumi and Tokyu Construction, have decided to wait before submitting a detailed work plan.
Consortium executives said the foreign members all want to do the tunnelling, but are trying to avoid the more technically problematic station work.
Theerapong said a detailed work plan could be submitted after the contract signing as was normal practice.
Ch Karnchang said its role in the project was primarily government liaison. "When we have a deal like this in our hands we have a reputation for not letting it get away," said a company executive.
Theerapong said bidding for a concessionaire to run the system and provide trains and fixtures would open next month. Initial investment costs are estimated at 11 billion baht (US$450 million).

He said relocation of a station encroaching on Bangkok's landmark Dusit Thani Hotel was not practical, but said a major concourse would be moved outside the hotel's grounds and construction disturbance would be minimalised.
Construction is due to start in the first quarter of 1997 for completion in 2002.
